posts.title: First Weeks: The Kids When They Were Tiny
posts.summary: Some of our first photos from the early days — when the kids were still small and everything felt brand new.

media.caption: Early kid season — the first little crew.
A snapshot from those first weeks.

body: These are a few of our first photos from when the kids were still tiny.
Those early days are equal parts joy and logistics: making sure everyone is warm, fed, and settling into the herd rhythm.
Lesson learned: take pictures early and often — it’s amazing how quickly they change, and it helps us keep our records straight as the herd grows.

posts.title: Meet Maduro
posts.summary: A photo from when we first got Maduro. The day he was captured in Venezuela made the name feel oddly appropriate.
body: This is Maduro — a photo from when we first got him.
The day he was captured in Venezuela, the name ‘Maduro’ seemed strangely fitting, so it stuck.
He’s been part of the rhythm here ever since — a steady presence and a good reminder that the farm has its own tempo.

posts.title: First Fire Pit Night
posts.summary: One of the first nights we completed our fire pit area — and burned some trash while we were at it.

media.caption: A short clip from the day the babies were born — nursing and settling in.

body: We finally completed our first fire pit area — one of those small milestones that makes the place feel more like home.
We also burned some trash that night (the practical side of farm work never really stops).
Lesson learned: progress is usually a stack of small nights like this, not one big weekend.

posts.title: Driveway Progress (700 ft)
posts.summary: Our ongoing driveway work — about 700 feet we’ve slowly cleared, and recently finished the apron work.
body: This is our ongoing driveway work — about 700 feet we’ve been slowly clearing and shaping over time.
We recently finished the apron work, which was a big step forward.
Lesson learned: long projects get done by showing up consistently. A little progress, then another little progress, and suddenly it’s real.

posts.title: First Milking Station (and a Lesson Learned)
posts.summary: We set up a small shelter to house a milking station and learned quickly that the pump machine wasn’t the right fit for us.

media.caption: A first look at the milking setup.
Buckets, supplies, and a learning curve.
We watched closely and adjusted quickly.
A calm moment in the station.

body: We built out a small shelter to house a milking station and gave milking a real attempt for the first time.
We tried a pump machine, but the pressure was inconsistent — either too much or not enough — and we could tell it was uncomfortable. We stopped immediately.
We returned the machine and switched to hand milking. It’s slower, but it’s gentler and gives us better control.
Lesson learned: comfort and consistency matter more than speed. We’ll optimize the process later — first we keep it humane and calm.

posts.title: Bingo (Green Collar)
posts.summary: This week we lost Bingo to anemia after weeks of supportive care. We’re recording what happened and what we learned.
body: This week we lost our goat Bingo (green collar) to anemia.
For weeks we tried to support her recovery with Red Cell and vitamin B, especially after using Cydectin. We kept working to get her eating and stronger, but unfortunately her body couldn’t recover.
We’re writing this down because these animals are part of our daily life, and because keeping records helps us improve how we care for the herd going forward.
Rest easy, Bingo.

posts.title: Roadway Progress (750+ ft) + Water Spickets Installed
posts.summary: Our 750+ ft roadway is coming together — we’re waiting on sod now, and we added water spickets along the strip to make watering and maintenance easier.

media.caption: Roadway progress — now waiting on sod.
Locia Farms sign installed at the entry.
Asphalt down — waiting on sod for the edges.

body: Our 750+ ft roadway is coming together. We’re now waiting on sod, but the shape and layout are really starting to feel finished.

One of the most useful upgrades in this stretch is the set of water spickets we added along the strip. My father-in-law did an amazing job creating them using polycarbonate tubing along the entire run.
It’s simple infrastructure, but it will make watering, maintenance, and future planting much easier — exactly the kind of steady, behind-the-scenes work that keeps a farm running well.
Update: the entry sign is up and the asphalt is down — next step is sod along the edges.
